maybe twelve meters. For an offshore structure in high

for a big, large floating island, with all these connected

winches, electronic winches controlled
by the GPS system and the water leveling system. The islands automatically correct
their position when they are carried
away by the current. During high tide
in the monsoon season, the system keeps
the islands level, above water. In normal time, the variation

And in flood time, it can move within ten meters... and high
ten meters... it is totally safe! If the construction of safe

so they can produce more locally, and we could reduce the food milesŧ
and then also reduce food losses. This is on a very small scale,
but yeah, you have to test it, and that is what we do over here. At the Rotterdam farm,
food is produced on the water in the middle
of the city. In Italy, a company is attempting
to farm under the sea. Nemo's garden
is the first ever underwater greenhouse experience
for humanity! So basically we are growing
plants underwater. We achieve it through a plastic dome,
and this half-sphere full with air is trapped
underwater, so basically... this is the surface...
this surface here! Inside this air, we have
a lot of buildup of the humidity that naturally is generated
by the evaporation of the sea. Because where does rain come from? We don't need to boil the sea,
we have evaporation, it's physics! It constantly happens slowly,
but it happens! And when the humidity
is high enough, it rains because it condenses
in clouds and precipitates. Inside the biosphere,
it's kind of similar. It's fresh! So it's drinkable? Yes. It's actually distilled! See, it's raining, now. Yeah. And, it has nutriment? We add the nutrients. So, we provide light thanks
to the Sun, now we have freshwater for free, automaticŧ We have
the pressure which is boosting the growth of our plants,
and you have stable temperature! The air cools off and warms up very
rapidly, but water takes more time! And when it heats
up, then it releases warmth slowly. It's very important for plants
to have stable temperature. So our greenhouse
does not need heating, and does not need
air conditioning. We have tested vegetables and fruits
of different kinds, so for example, strawberries,
pumpkins, there's so many... we had a great success with beans! Soil is very precious and rare
in the world, but we don't need soil because the seed is good
on a substrate that is a holder! It can of coconut fibers,
of material that you can recycle from other biological waste...
In the case of our plastic, which is methacrylate, it's a kind
of material that does not release molecules in the water,
and these domes are reusable for years. We understand that our product
is gonna be more expensive than something grown
on land. Hopefully, this alternative will scale
up to a moment where the price is not going to be that much more. If we find a way to create
an alternative for agriculture, which is sustainable,
which uses resources in a responsible way, then bingo! We have a solution, or part

is the scarcity of drinking water. Is it possible to desalinate

for energy, we have a mechanism at the water's surface,

potable, and each unit can supply some 5,000
liters per day. The first of these plants was
deployed by a coastal city in Chile. But research is continuing,
because the cost of the water supplied

in partnership with the United Nations, is preparing

to fly to the moon and to space. That is now part of human history. That's why I believe we can take

city, they can see how it complements the existing city and waterfront.

you have landscape features, you have the flow of a river,
and the riverbanks that you build along. You have the waterfront

also somehow inform the direction
of the streets. So when you're building at the sea,
you are potentially directionless! And therefore we thought
of this idea of the hexagon,
could be multidirectional. Those spaces can then contain
water management, power storage, water filtration and even
in-construction agriculture! It does sound
a little science-fictionesque, but you know, one of the most
beautiful cities on Earth, Venice, it's built in the water,
on piles. Originally for defensive purposes,
and then it became an advantage that all the streets are paved with water! Let's just say, like,
one of the most amazing cities we know
of is entirely in the water! And in that sense,
Oceanix... the idea of floating cities could be like 
a 21st-century equivalent of the... of the marvel of human engineering
and imagination that is Venice today! So the idea is to start
with a floating prototype in Busan...
inside a protected natural harbor! And for now, the purpose
of Oceanix is to develop an urban toolkit that can then
be delivered at scale! If floating cities could be built
from toolkits, this could also pave the way
for private cities located out on the open
sea and beyond government control. This caters

governments give them. Seasteading is a new utopian
and libertarian project. It's all about taking
the idea of living freely and taking
it into deep water! And the ultimate goal
is complete freedom. And of course that sounds quite
attractive, but when one also thinks it's freedom for people who are
wealthy, it's freedom for people who have a highly developed
libertarian capitalist ideology. This isn't a vision for everybody,
and it's not a vision for the masses! It's a vision that caters
for the few. Two hundred nautical miles
from any border, the nation-state still has some power
but beyond that, you have the high seas! They knew that no state
could get to them. You can, if you've established
a country on the high seas, be free from any police force, any military,
you would have complete autonomy! And that is what
the seasteaders want. They want their freedom
to start their own society, according
to their own rules. Storms are particularly
bad in the high seas. The height
of waves can be tremendous. A structure wouldn't last very long

into calmer waters. And that's why the seasteaders have

shallow waters in order for their structures to sustain themselves

the Seasteading Institute was looking for in the lagoons
of French Polynesia in 2017. For the American group
from Silicon Valley, it was the ideal place
to build a floating settlement far away from regulations,
and close enough for stability. We were involved in a floating island
for French Polynesia - a very interesting project, fully based
on a zero environmental impact, completely self-supporting
systems... Yeah, very interesting! Unfortunately,

enough by the local communities. For its supporters, the project
was a response to rising sea levels and an opportunity
for economic growth. For opponents,
however, it was a gateway for foreign investors
to serve their own interests. Look how peaceful it is here,
and now they're ruining it with these floating islands. We have nothing left. Everything will be polluted,
afterwards. Every morning we come here to fish. We have our traditions. And now they're taking all that
away from us? I can't believe it. We only heard that boats
are no longer allowed to go out within
a certain radius. They are not even subject
to our labor laws. But who will work here
and who will still want to benefit
from our beautiful lagoon? We would not even
be allowed to sail our boats past the floating
islands anymore. We in Tahiti live from fishing. Everyone here has their own boat
and goes fishing, sometimes at night. And what could you catch there? There's the floating island,
which disturbs everything. For these American investors,
all of whom are super-rich billionaires,
everything can be bought for them. A government, a mayor,
a politician... simply everything. It was here, one here, one there
and another one there. There were three zones. I had read about it in the press
and seen that Monsieur Bouissou, the former vice president, had
already signed his letter of intent. We saw photos of our mayor showing
the Americans, the billionaires, around the entire lagoon, and that's
when we realized that our government had already entered into partnerships
with American investors from Silicon Valley who belong
to a kind of sect and call themselves libertarians. No one ever listened to us. I myself was a member
of the Polynesian Parliament at the time, and the government
never discussed it with us. It wasn't a dream,
it was a real nightmare. The idea of waking
up in the morning and seeing a floating island
in our lagoon... I don't know. We understand them. They want to go to beautiful places. But they also have to understand us. This is our home. I don't just come
into your home and settle in, saying,
"Hey, make some room." No, it doesn't work like that. For us, it was a very
colonialist approach. Self-supporting gated community
out there in the ocean that has nothing to do with other people
- that's not how I see it! So I see it more
as a symbiotic relationship between the city on the water
and the city on the land! Always, in human history
we have had those who have been bold and innovative. What may seem today
is a utopia will probably become a reality
in the next years. It's more economic to build on land
than it is to create a floating city. So a floating city is likely only
to happen out of absolute necessity! Unless somebody decides that
as an experiment, it is worth that level of investment
to demonstrate that potential. I don't see a city
in the future where we are completely on the open water,
with nothing else around us! I really see it always in combination
of cities on land. Where we can expect these floating
cities in the future is always be in the high-density cities
around the world! Shanghai, Tokyo, New York, Miami,
everywhere where there is a threat of water, where the city is not that
high, where there's a need of space, there, I think it's logical that's
that cities will grow over the water! I am convinced
that in the coming century we will live, much more,
on and under the sea. It is like a sixth continent,
something to benefit all of humanity.

why people have their laundry done here—even today, in the 21st century. Some people may have a
washing machine, but no water. You don’t get as much water,
nor as clean water, from the tap. Where do you get the water? We get the water from
the city administration. They supply it for Dhobi Ghat. So, many houses
don’t have water in them? No, they don’t get
that kind of water. We use the same water
for drinking and washing. Officially, Mumbai’s water
is clean enough to drink. But there are several snags. Millions of people are not connected
to the mains water supply and get their water from supply trucks. The quality and supply vary
greatly depending on the quality of maintenance of the mains network. In Dhobi Ghat, the city
administration has ensured that everything is in order, because
the washers here are really needed in the city. We wash approximately
450 items per day. 450 pieces? On your own? No, there are three of us
working—me, my son, and my wife. 7,000 laundry workers and their
families live and work in Dhobi Ghat, united in a cooperative that has
a degree of bargaining power with the city administration. Most of the people here are migrant

seek their fortune in Mumbai, often going back generations. First my grandfather came because

father later came to Mumbai as well. After that, our situation
improved, so we settled here. Now things are fine. Laundry is washed, dried, and ironed
around the clock in Dhobi Ghat, with more than 100,000 items of
laundry processed every day. How much can he and his family earn

in their home province, but most of it is invested in
their children’s education. People in the higher castes
have it better; we belong to the lower castes. Nevertheless, we continue

artist is in the bridal industry. I’m not going to lie. Customers pay the equivalent of

a single session. Daniel Bauer’s style is in demand,
and here in India, money is no object when it comes to weddings,

not fun, it’s hard work. What are your expectations,
your hopes, your wishes? I don’t expect anything. I just want to give my 100 percent. That’s it. I don’t hope anything. Duty rather than pleasure. The wedding day is the most important

family– 40 to 50 lakhs. 40 to 50 lakhs? Yes. That’s an average party. That includes jewelry, the

people come and stay there. They have their different cultures,
they brought their cultures, they brought their lifestyles. In Mumbai, we have
the whole of India here. Basically, it is a
mini-India, staying in a small place called Mumbai. Very small place Mumbai,
that’s how it works out. A small place? Well, everything is relative. Amruta and her family are another
reason why Mumbai is so special. A simple apartment
building in the middle of the city. The apartment where Amruta grew up
with her brother and parents is on the fifth floor. Fifty square meters, one and a half
rooms, everything has a function in this very small space. Her father came as an orphan from the
countryside, where there was no food and no work for him. He sought to improve
his fortunes in Mumbai. Times were hard, and you can sense
how proud the children are of their father– who managed to
become a vegetable trader. He came to Mumbai, and just under the
bridges he spent his days, for a few years, and he used to go to the
common toilets to freshen himself. Their mother worked as a maid. Their parents worked hard so that
their children would have a better life and invested
everything in their education. Mumbai made that possible. Whatever we are today, how should I
put this: both of us went to common school just because of both of them. Because he couldn’t afford but
he made sure that his children had a better life. Today, their son is the social

to learn how to ride a motorcycle. I searched on Google is there any motor-
cycle or driving school that do for women. So then I came to know that this is the
gap that we have to fill in the society, because many of the women in the
society are looking for such training schools where they are not comfortable with
the male instructors but more comfortable with the women instructors. At the age of 21, she
founded her first driving school, Women on Wheels. A motorcycle driving
school exclusively for women. Today, at the age of 27, it has
expanded to four driving schools. She wants to expand further from
Mumbai to the neighboring province and then across the entire country. She has already trained more than
5,000 women, including many female police officers in Mumbai. She organizes women-only
motorcycle events and trips across the vast country. And everything she does is about more
than just riding motorcycles—she wants to help modernize Indian
society: I am the voice of many women in the society, who really wants to
have that independence on motorcycle, or not just motorcycle, but
independence within herself that yes, she can ride and she can actually
go out and do everything on herself without depending on somebody else. And so our journey through the night
ends with a young woman and her family, who represent everything that
Mumbai, this extraordinary megacity, stands for: hope, courage, and
openness, hard work, and above all, a zest for life.

important in Greenland. But we’re not allowed
to compete independently. The only way talented soccer

A mother visits the grave of her son – who died after a brutal assault. I don't know, I … I can't believe … that
my son's down there. It's always awful being here. I don't believe he's actually here.
It's just what's left on this Earth. I think he's floating around
somewhere, looking down on us. Philip's death
has made Joanna question everything – including her faith. That God allowed

Joanna's daughter and Philip's sister. The whole family were looking
forward to an unforgettable evening. The party was … just wonderful – and we had a lot of fun. It was actually the
first time I'd ever seen my son on the dancefloor! We had a fantastic time. At around 2 a.m.
Philip left the party together with
his best friend Max. The two of them
had been inseparable ever since elementary school. While waiting for

 was her son: critically injured,

check whether they were wearing them under their skirts. If a girl was caught, she could be beaten and

the pants were forbidden. It was very violent back then." The traditional garment survived
through decades of repression. They're made by hand
in Ribnovo to this day. They're for daily wear, too not just special occasions. The younger generation
is keeping up the tradition. Easily half of the girls wear
their red trousers to school. Shurfe Molaalieva and
Fatme Avdikova remember the communist era very well. It was enforced
uniformity, they say. Anything differing from
the norm was unwelcome. "Once, I went to the
city of Gotse Delchev. Because I was wearing
traditional clothing and a headscarf, they refused to let
me ride the bus." "I remember when we went
out to the fields for the harvest. Some men came yelling at us
that we were wearing our shalvari under our skirts. They told us to take them off. A woman came over: 'Why are you yelling like that? Let me see what you
have under your pants! Pull your pants down!' The men left us
alone after that." "It's better now. Nobody says anything, nobody
bothers you, nobody insults you. They're happy and
proud that their tradition has survived for
thousands of years. The resilient
Pomaks are an ethno-confessional
minority in Bulgaria, with an estimated
300,000 Bulgarian Muslims. Mustafa's mother is getting a
wedding dress ready for the visitor from Great Britain,
Eleanor Potter. She's been invited to try it on. "I love dressing up, so this is kind
of something I've never worn before." "This is something
very special." "The detail on the
clothes is so beautiful. Do you make it yourself?" "Yeah." "So for the wedding,
every dress is different?" "And is this the clothes
that the bride wears all day?" "Yeah, actually not all days only at weddings
or let's say Fridays." "I'm very privileged
to be treated this way. I appreciate that." "You can feel the
heart in these garments, because it's part of their
culture that is passed from generation to generation. So I just, I love clothes,
because to me it is art and culture." Mustafa drives to a
neighboring village where there are
a number of hotels something his own village lacks. That is why so few tourists
have come to Ribnovo up to now and he’d like to change that. "Two mountain ranges
meet in this region. The air is pure, there
are ski resorts nearby. There are also mineral springs here,
which can be good for your health. All of that makes our region
attractive as a vacation destination all year round." He's come to meet the
manager of Hotel Leshten, whom he's begun
a collaboration with. Yoanna Petkanina
has plenty of guests; he has a one-of-a-kind
wedding ritual. It's good cause
to work together. Yoanna has a group
of students arriving who want to experience
a Ribnovo wedding. "It's a chance for
them to experience something
truly interesting. It could be an
enriching experience. It's much better to see
something new on vacation. Something different,
something emotional rather than the typical
vacation with spa, pool, sauna. You can get that
almost anywhere. The wedding, on the other hand that sets our region
apart from the rest." This is Mustafa's favorite
spot, very close to Ribnovo. He hopes to entice tourists from
all over the world to come here. "We'll build a slice of
paradise here in Bulgaria. Over there's Bansko
resort with ski facilities, down there the
Ognyanovo mineral springs. Then the Aegean Sea and Greece. We'll have paths for
electric motorcycles and bicycles for
teenagers and children. There'll be tents and
yurts for overnight guests." Day two of the wedding. Now comes the bride's day; it's her relatives who are
invited to the celebration. In shifts, as always. Meleim Menkov and Nevse
Kiselova are also hopeful that tourism in
Ribnovo will create jobs. Like so many men here,
Meleim is a seasonal worker. He's away in Spain for months
at a time working on the harvest. It's one reason weddings here
are held more often in winter. Fabric for 80 pairs
of red trousers, as well as 150 slippers
and 47 blankets. The tourists are amazed
at the sheer volume, which the women of
Ribnovo are happy to explain. "Well, yes. It's a lot. But it's better to have a lot. It's always better
to have more." One tourist wants
to know more... "Are you already saving up?" "Yes. These are my daughters, here. I have two." "That means dowries for two?" "Yes, of course." "Everything's beautiful,
all of it will be useful. Come on, show me what you like." "These are my favorites. For a girl." "It doesn't matter which. The main thing
is that it's healthy." "My eldest daughter
is getting married. I can't describe the feeling,
you'd have to experience it. Maybe tomorrow I'll
be able to say more. Right now, we're sad.
Well, I should go now. I still have a lot
of work to do." "We met in a café. Almost three years ago. I knew, 'She was
the one for me!'" The groom accompanies
the bride to her family home. Now, the most exciting
part of the ritual can begin. Mustafa has another
appointment in Sofia. To have the Pomak wedding
ritual recognized by UNESCO, he'll also need
academic support. He has found that in the
form of Veselka Toncheva, associate professor at the
Institute of Ethnology and Folklore at the Bulgarian
Academy of Sciences. She focuses on the
ritual's authenticity an important
criterion for UNESCO. "What makes it important? What makes it authentic? Can it be considered
a living tradition? It's absolutely alive! In that village, we
don't have to prove it you can see it! The tradition lives
on in that village. When girls are born, they begin
collecting for the 'cheiz,' the dowry the things they will take with
them into their husband's house." With 30 fellow advocates, Mustafa
formed a foundation for the project. He couldn't manage it all alone. "The foundation is so we
can finance community events and keep developments
rolling along. We've built a
fundraising team, too, so we can pursue important
goals for the local community." It's early evening
on the second day. Many of the bride's family
members gather at her parents' house. It’s time for the bride
to become the 'Gelina' meaning 'bright light.' Nevse has held her
eyes closed for hours now. It's only from attending
other weddings that she knows
what she looks like but not the details. Each Gelina receives her
own unique face painting. For her mother, it's a
very emotional moment. "How I feel… I don't know." The older members
of the family see that, while the ritual itself
has remained the same, some things have
changed with time. "Now, there's more money. Things are better. It's not like it used to be. Back then when we got
married, there wasn't any music." This extraordinary
ritual has persisted, replaced by neither
Christianity nor Islam. It's what makes it so special. The ethnic community in
Ribnovo has held on to it. The Gelina is
presented to her village. Then she's led, eyes still closed,
all the way to the groom's home. She carries the mirror with her the
whole way, as a spiritual metaphor. "The life of a girl in Ribnovo has
stages that begin with her birth and culminate in her
becoming a Gelina. She keeps her eyes closed so
she doesn't see what lies ahead. The mirror reflects her past. That's what she'd see if she
accidentally opens her eyes while walking. She can only see
what's already happened. When she reaches
her husband's house, that's the moment when
she meets her future." Nevse is led into
Meleim's parental home. Relatives stream into the house, which bursts at the seams
with so many visitors. Once again, people
arrive in shifts. It's an exhausting
ritual, and very elaborate. And yet, this time-honored
tradition is a growing trend. "You don't have to
get married this way, but more and more
young people want to. It’s a tradition that brings
everyone in Ribnovo together and strengthens the bond
of a newly formed family. Because everyone is involved from preparing the cheiz, the
dowry, to painting the Gelina, all the way to the
religious ceremony. That's what brings the
community together." The groom removes
the bride's makeup. Then, she's allowed to
open her eyes to look ahead, into this new
chapter of her life. Ribnovo is two-and-a-half
hours from Sofia. After the wedding,
Mustafa travels back there. He still has a lot of work
ahead of him on the project. "Once we're recognized
as national cultural heritage, we can begin the
process to have it accepted as UNESCO Intangible
Cultural Heritage. We have to make a
video that documents our tradition for
the application. Then the Ministry of Culture, together with the
Ministry of Foreign Affairs, will officially submit the UNESCO application for the
Ribnovo wedding tradition." In two years, Mustafa is hopeful
they'll have reached their goal. Meanwhile, they’ll
keep on celebrating.

Will they still be fishing then? We ask the captain of another cutter
whose catch is just being unloaded. If things go on like
this, we're on our way out. The fishing quota is too low,
the fish are dirt cheap and diesel far too expensive.
It's bad, really bad. I can hardly look my
crew in the eye anymore. It makes me sick. And I need to spend a fortune on
repairs to the boat: 70, 80 thousand
euros just for maintenance! If this was Spain or France,
there’d be a thousand boats here. But here, there’s just a
few dozen of us… Too few to be important–
their future looks bleak without largescale change, say Mestre Eduino
and his brother Paulo. They’re returning to their
home port on the island of Pico. Their crew members
are seasonal workers from Portugal’s former colonies. Very few locals are
up for doing the job. Even though the two brothers
will have no income for the next two months, they still have to pay
the minimum wage, social security contributions, insurance and
food for their crew. Their father, who once also fished
on this boat, predicted this would happen… Before he died, he told us:
Sell the cutter, before you lose it along with your house
and everything you own. Mestre Eduino arrives with
his 14-year-old son Vicente. He also has another older son
who left the island and works for an insurance company
in northern Portugal. I don't want my younger
son to be a fisherman either. He should go to
university and find a good job. If he likes fishing, then he
should do it for sport, but not as a profession, I don't
want that for him. Once I finish high school,
I want to study electrical engineering in Lisbon. It's a similar story in Paulo's
family: They live in Santa Cruz das Ribeiras, a traditional
fishing village in Pico. We used to have five tuna
boats here in the village and all the crews were from here. Today, I’m the only one
still fishing for tuna. At the same time, the
number of tourists visiting the Azores is growing. Apart from diving, the
islands are popular with hikers too. That’s my granddaughter. Paulo's only son is a math teacher
on the main island of Sao Miguel. He comes to Pico regularly to visit
his parents and see his daughter. He didn't want his
father's job either. He believes the current focus
on tourism alone is risky: We’re concentrating solely
on this sector while greatly restricting others that also have potential. Fishing was once the island’s
engine of economic development. Many people earned a living
from it and families built their homes
with the income. Today we’re losing
that, and I find that sad. What's more, says Rodrigo, the
tourists don’t want to see empty villages and deserted streets either. You could go to a museum, where
a video shows you what life was once like here. But today
you can just watch that on YouTube, you don't have to fly
to the middle of the Atlantic. What future do the Azores have? Mestre Eduino fears it’s
unlikely to include tuna fishing.

you know, that was fine. If she wanted to spend time there,

convicted of murdering German photographer Anja Niedringhaus

and said: "You got to be kidding me. You can't… You can go off to war, but
you can't make it through a speech in a church? What's the matter with
you?" You know, she was tough. Tough woman. We are adrift in a sea of grief. We do not want to let go of Anja. We cannot let go of Anja. She was so, so alive. Anja and I used to joke, and I would
say: Now, if anything happens, I want you to say really
nice things about me. And she said: Never mind if it's me,
I want you to be sure to make sure you say this or you say that. I wasn't able to go to the funeral
because I was in Germany, but I was in the hospital. I was able to send something over to
be read at the funeral, but I wasn't able to go. I wasn't able to
leave the hospital at all. I close my eyes, and I see you smile. I close my eyes,
and I hear you laugh. We were a hell of a team. I remember some of your last words. "I am so happy," you said. I love you, mein Schatz. I miss you.

operators look well maintained, and carry FSC certification. Laschefski wants to hear
more from the local residents. Salete is the leader
of this community. "It's gotten so bad that
our wells have dried up. We had to give up our livestock. Things kept getting worse, and
now it's really very hard to survive." Salete wants to
show us something related to the FSC
certification report. "This used to be a rushing stream
that had water all year round." Today, the stream is dry. Yet the FSC report reaches
a different conclusion. Documents show that
the FSC was informed in writing several
times about this case, and about similar
incidents in the region. Still, the report
concludes that the allegations could
not be substantiated. "This is a clear violation
of the FSC's first principle: respect for human rights. Access to water
is a human right. And here, that right is clearly
being denied to these communities. By certifying this, the FSC
is violating its own rules." When asked, the FSC
cited Aperam's certification, said it knew of no confirmed
violations by ArcelorMittal, and welcomed information
on possible breaches. Aperam stated that its
plantations comply with the highest environmental
and social standards, rejecting claims of greenwashing
and human rights violations. In one of Brazil's poorest
regions, the situation remains dire. Reforestation,
meant as a solution, is causing suffering
and deepening divisions. "This is a place where people give
thanks for having escaped suffering. But it also stands for how much
suffering there has been here, and how much still exists. People disappear from
their farms without a trace. Bodies are found. People are run over, and it's never clear whether it
was an accident or deliberate. All of this is extremely,
extremely stressful." So what will happen to the
people now facing displacement by the plantations? "It feels like the calm
before the storm." Then an emergency call reaches
the lawyer André Alves da Souza. In Pindaíba, part of the
Cerrado is being cleared, without authorization. In just one day, an area the size of
1,600 soccer pitches is destroyed. "The community
is defending itself. This camp is meant
to protect their land. People will stay until the
courts take up the case day and night to defend what's theirs." In the early morning hours,
heavy machinery moved in, accompanied by police. They were not there to protect the
people, or the natural environment. "The police don't intervene. People feel abandoned, and are
taking matters into their own hands." This cellphone footage shows what
follows environmental destruction: violence and counter-violence. That day, the people of Pindaíba managed
to push the plantation workers back. "It was desperation. They don't even
see us as human." At first, it felt
like a victory. But it didn't last long. Now, the people of Pindaíba themselves
are facing accusations of violence. "They destroy everything
and we're left here in misery. "In Europe and the U.S., you talk about carbon neutrality,
but it doesn't really exist." "There used to be
deer and armadillos here. My father warned
us about jaguars. It's all gone, and that hurts." Despite all this human
suffering, could plantations
still play a role in fighting the
climate crisis? Klemens Laschefski
wants answers. Deep inside the plantations,
he makes a discovery: a cleared area belonging to
the steel company GERDAU. Just beyond it are hundreds of brick
huts, smoke rising from each one. Charcoal ovens. "The eucalyptus that's
supposed to store carbon is burned almost immediately. Turned into charcoal. It's unbelievable. Four hundred charcoal
burners, all smoking away. A war on nature." Trees meant to act as carbon
sinks are cut down and burned, releasing the CO2 they stored. The charcoal is then
loaded onto trucks. "That raises the
obvious question: how is this climate protection?" How can reforestation carried
out in the name of climate protection end up destroying
natural habitats, and fueling charcoal
production instead? Laschefski follows the trucks
as they leave the plantations, passing vast mining
sites and iron ore mines. The journey continues along
the endless roads of the Cerrado. Again and again, trucks
loaded with charcoal appear. Eventually, they converge here. "There are a lot
of ore trucks here. And coal trucks. This is where the charcoal
meets the iron ore." Fire, smoke, and searing
heat are everywhere, across the entire valley. Above it all, a dome of pollution
hangs over the landscape. This is where the
charcoal trail ends: in the furnaces of iron
and steel production. Here, iron ore is turned into
pellets using heat generated by burning charcoal
made from eucalyptus. "The charcoal produced across
hundreds of thousands of hectares in northern Minas is simply
burned again right here." The plants run around the clock. Their product is in demand. So-called "lower-carbon"
iron ore pellets, produced using what the industry
calls "sustainable charcoal." The trail now leads to Europe
and the German port of Hamburg, where pellets
from Brazil arrive. Arne Langner works
for ArcelorMittal, one of the world's
largest steel producers. The company
operates mines and eucalyptus plantations
in Minas Gerais. "These are iron ore pellets
from Brazil or Canada. They come from our own mines,
extracted to our highest standards, pelletized there, and then shipped to Europe." So-called "green" steel is
being promoted as the future, and as an opportunity for
German industry to demonstrate its climate credentials. Flames roar in the
furnace as metal is melted to produce what's often
described as "climate-friendly" steel. Then we notice a familiar name: GERDAU. The Brazilian corporation
alleged to be linked to plantation operators
involved in land conflicts with the community of Pindaíba. So what role does
GERDAU play in supposedly cleaner steel
production in Germany? That's a question Arne
Langner doesn't answer. The German market is set
to embrace "green" steel. Hamburg's public
transport authority is one of the
major customers. Its U5 subway line project
aims to set new benchmarks including for
sustainable construction. "We only use green steel. We have very clear requirements
for our construction companies and suppliers. Our tenders now
include annual checks of what's available
on the market. And if greener steel is
available on the market, companies are
required to use it here." "That helps the market grow. Hamburg is leading the way. That's great. We need more
projects like this." ArcelorMittal points to
comprehensive environmental audits, a whistleblower system,
and FSC certification and says it is not aware of
any environmental problems or complaints linked to its
eucalyptus plantations in Brazil. On a scientific level, however, Dietrich Darr and Katrin
Meinhold can now provide answers and clarity. "The results are pretty clear. We've found around 30 to
40 species in the undergrowth and shrub layer of the
eucalyptus plantations." So how many plant
species are in the Cerrado? "The Cerrado has
three times as many. We've identified more
than 100 different species. That gives us a very clear picture,
and it backs up, with hard data, what we already suspected
when we were out there." "What's key is that
roughly half of the biomass and a large share of the carbon is stored underground,
in the roots." The Cerrado's secret: it's an inverted forest. Its roots store far more CO2
than the plantations above ground. For the first time, the scientists hear about the
other strands of research carried out for this film. "If ecosystems in Brazil are
being destroyed so the West can keep producing steel and that steel is then
given a green label that's completely absurd." The World Bank plays
a key role in promoting reforestation initiatives and
carbon offset mechanisms. For this documentary, officials responsible for
these programs agree to meet with Klemens Laschefski. "The carbon market
was originally intended to make it possible
for poorer countries to finance the transition
to a sustainable economy. That was the idea behind it." "In principle, the World Bank
set this process in motion. And it's triggered an
enormous number of conflicts." "I was there. I managed the project. And I have to
disagree, at least in part. Brazil is the only country with
steel production that is sustainable, or partly sustainable. About ten percent is
produced using charcoal instead of lignite or brown coal. And that charcoal comes
from eucalyptus plantations, which are intended
to replace fossil fuels. This was the first
sustainable plantation aimed at replacing fossil fuels
in the steel industry." Destroying the Cerrado,
replacing it with eucalyptus, and then burning those trees to
make charcoal for the steel industry. Is that really sustainable? "This project was examined
by a whole range of NGOs. There were no conflicts." This film has
documented conflicts. So why does the World Bank
refuse to acknowledge them? The World Bank
official places the responsibility
with the certifiers, including the FSC. "We have to rely on the FSC, on the fact that all seven
certification processes we’ve had are working. These certification processes
have to be implemented as intended." Responsibility is
shifted elsewhere. And the consequences. "It shows a huge gap
between aspiration and reality, maybe even an illusion
people want to preserve. I wouldn't want to
say it was deliberate. I'm sure he experienced things the
way he described them, in good faith. But what I saw was
something very different." The World Bank has since
announced investments of more than 250 million euros in
Aperam's eucalyptus plantations in Minas Gerais. There are plans to
expand them by 25 percent. These are the very plantations
threatening Salete and her community. So will governments
have the courage to pursue genuine
environmental protection? In any case, the World
Bank has another proposal. "The Brazilian government has taken
up a proposal from the World Bank. The Tropical
Forests Forever Fund. The idea is to create
an investment fund worth several hundred
billion dollars." The World Bank says it
takes all allegations relating to environmental and
social impacts very seriously. Money may offer answers
at the level of global politics. But for the
families of Pindaíba, it means they must
continue to worry about the future
of their children. "The Cerrado used
to be everywhere. It was so dense, you
couldn't even walk through it."

## 46. Sausage stands and coffee houses - When night falls in Vienna | DW Documentary

The Austrian capital of Vienna. A historic and modern city resting
on the banks of the Danube river. Vienna draws millions of visitors
each year and was ranked the world’s second most livable city in 2015. But what remains when the
tourists turn in for the night? That’s when the city reveals many of

success has two parts. And the first is
that the party’s wild. Or that it’s unforgiveable.

a little different here. One guest at a funeral
actually refused to shake my hand. He thought if he did, he’d be next. Vienna changes at night. You notice it first in the
city’s famed coffee houses. There’s a point when I ask guests
that order an Americano if it’s a coffee or a cocktail! Austria’s largest city is home
to just under two million people. The Viennese may not always show it,
but they have many sides: They can be warm, Or playful. Vienna can be depressing, enchanting
Or completely out of control– when the night falls… Our tour of
night-time Vienna begins in the city’s eighth district at 9:30pm. We enter the MMM Espresso bar
off the “Gürtel”, or belt, Vienna’s main traffic artery. Unimpressive from the outside–

but came to Vienna over 40 years ago - and fell in love:
with the city, and this bar. It’s now legendary–
and we soon find out why. It’s a little piece of the
Balkans– right here in Austria. Many who now call Vienna
home came from the former Yugoslavia, like Mitra. The country had historic ties to
the former Austro-Hungarian empire. People from all over met
in Vienna, including in 3M. When we had the last war in
Yugoslavia, for example, Serbs, Muslims, Croats, Albanians,
were all at war with each other. Over there. But not here. Here we were all together, here we
have Serbian songs, Croatian songs. I had two Muslim waitresses.
I had a Muslim singer. And I never had any problems. How did she keep the deep divisions
of war from spilling over here? Mitra has a big heart–
and incredibly good ears. People would be sat around. And I have a gift, I can be sitting
in one place, and if four people are sitting over there, I can
hear what they’re talking about. I thought, if they start discussing

your family, and all of you who’ve been coming
here for years! Thank you! An old former boss,

Will she leave Vienna? Maybe she’ll tell us later. Many of the city's streets are

have settled in Berlin, trying to rebuild a new life. Sasha also lives in Berlin. She looks towards
a free future with her partner, Sonia. She performs in concerts and exhibits the drawings
she made while in detention. Zhenya and Sveta
have been separated, transferred to women's prisons
hundreds of kilometers from Moscow. Arseny has been sent
to a juvenile penal colony in the Urals.
